parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about a sample with billions of nuclei - you can predict the average rate, but what can you say about one specific nucleus and when it will decay?
parts.proper_answer: Random means it cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay, or which nucleus will decay next.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Random Really Means**
Think of sitting next to a huge crowd of unstable nuclei. You know that as a whole they decay at a steady average rate, but for any one individual nucleus there is no pattern, no warning and no way to tell when its turn will come. That complete unpredictability for the individual nucleus is what we call random.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about whether heating, cooling, squeezing or changing chemical surroundings can trigger or stop a nucleus from decaying.
parts.proper_answer: Spontaneous means decay is not affected by external factors such as temperature, pressure or chemical environment.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Spontaneous Really Means**
Spontaneous means it happens on its own without needing a trigger. Changing temperature, pressure, chemical state or surroundings makes no difference to the chance of decay. The nucleus decays entirely by itself when it is ready.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at what is plotted: $\ln(A/\text{Bq})$ against $t$. A straight line with negative slope tells you the original curve was exponential - how does taking logs turn it into a straight line?
Hint 2: Read two widely spaced points off the straight line in Fig. 12.1 and use them to find the magnitude of the gradient. What does that gradient represent physically?
Hint 3: Once you have the decay constant $\lambda$, recall how $\lambda$ is linked to half-life $T_{1/2}$. Remember to keep $\lambda$ in $\text{min}^{-1}$ if you want $T_{1/2}$ in minutes.
parts.proper_answer: From $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, $\ln A = \ln A_0 - \lambda t$ so gradient $= -\lambda \approx -0.070\text{ min}^{-1}$. $T_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \lambda \approx 10\text{ min}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Turn The Exponential Into A Straight Line**
You know activity falls exponentially: $$A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$ Taking natural logs of both sides gives: $$\ln A = \ln A_0 - \lambda t$$ That is in the form $y = c + mx$, so a plot of $\ln A$ against $t$ is a straight line with gradient $m = -\lambda$ and intercept $\ln A_0$.

Step 2: **Find Lambda From The Gradient**
Read off the line. At $t = 0$, $\ln(A/\text{Bq}) \approx 36.4$. At $t = 20\text{ min}$, $\ln(A/\text{Bq}) \approx 35.0$. So: $$\lambda = -\text{gradient} = -\frac{35.0 - 36.4}{20 - 0} = \frac{1.4}{20} \approx 0.070\text{ min}^{-1}$$ A quicker equivalent is to note that a fall of $\ln 2 = 0.693$ in $\ln A$ corresponds to one half-life.

Step 3: **Convert To Half-Life**
Half-life and decay constant are linked by: $$T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$ Put in $\lambda$ in $\text{min}^{-1}$ to get $T_{1/2}$ directly in minutes: $$T_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{0.070} \approx 9.9\text{ min} \approx 10\text{ min}$$ You can check this on the graph: $\ln A$ falls from 36.4 to $36.4 - 0.693 = 35.7$ in about 10 min.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: mass, nucleon number and atomic mass unit
hints: Hint 1: Start from the link between how active the sample is and how many unstable nuclei it contains. Which equation connects activity $A$, decay constant $\lambda$ and number $N$?
Hint 2: Use the intercept of Fig. 12.1 at $t = 0$ to find the initial activity $A_0$. How do you undo a natural log? Remember to convert $\lambda$ from part (i) to $\text{s}^{-1}$ for SI units.

Hint 3: The total mass is $N$ times the mass of one atom, and one atom has mass approx nucleon number $\times$ $u$, where $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$. How can you rearrange to find nucleon number?
parts.proper_answer: $A_0 = e^{36.4} \approx 6.4 \times 10^{15}\text{ Bq}$, $\lambda \approx 1.17 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$, $N_0 = A_0/\lambda \approx 5.5 \times 10^{18}$. Mass per atom $= 5.66 \times 10^{-7}/N_0$, nucleon number $\approx 62$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Activity To Number Of Nuclei**
Activity is the rate of decay: $$A = \lambda N$$ At $t = 0$ this gives $N_0 = A_0 / \lambda$. You already have $\lambda$ from part (i), but convert it to per second because activity $A$ is in $\text{Bq} = \text{s}^{-1}$: $$\lambda = 0.070\text{ min}^{-1} = \frac{0.070}{60}\text{ s}^{-1} \approx 1.17 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}^{-1}$$

Step 2: **Find The Initial Activity From The Graph**
The intercept at $t = 0$ is $\ln(A_0/\text{Bq}) = 36.4$, so undo the log: $$A_0 = e^{36.4}\text{ Bq} \approx 6.4 \times 10^{15}\text{ Bq}$$ Then the number of X atoms at $t = 0$ is: $$N_0 = \frac{A_0}{\lambda} = \frac{6.4 \times 10^{15}}{1.17 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 5.5 \times 10^{18}$$

Step 3: **Use Mass To Find Nucleon Number**
Total mass $=$ number $\times$ mass of one atom. Mass of one atom $\approx A_r \times u$, where $A_r$ is the nucleon number and $u = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$: $$m = N_0 A_r u$$ Rearrange: $$A_r = \frac{m}{N_0 u} = \frac{5.66 \times 10^{-7}}{(5.5 \times 10^{18})(1.66 \times 10^{-27})} \approx 62$$ So nuclide X has nucleon number about 62.
